This file is used only during development by [dotnet run], [dotnet watch], and [Visual Studio Code]; it is not published. Let’s comment on it:

  • lines 3–4: A launch profile describes a way to launch the application. There is only one here; [dotnet run] uses the first one;
  • line 5: the application is launched directly, with its own web server;
  • lines 6–7: [dotnet run] displays its compilation messages, and the browser opens to the application when it is ready;
  • line 8: the listening address, the same as the key [Urls] from [appsettings.json]. When launched via this profile, the application uses this address; when launched outside the profile (for example, once published), it uses the address from [appsettings.json];
  • Lines 9–10: the environment variables passed to the application. [ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development] sets the environment: [appsettings.Development.json] is read, and the commands in SQL are displayed. On a production server, without this file or this variable, the environment is [Production].

docs.title: 11.6.5. Config/AuthOptions.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Config/AuthOptions.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The "Auth" section of appsettings.json, in the form of a typed class.
//
// This is the "options pattern" for ASP.NET Core: in
// Program.cs, builder.Services.Configure<AuthOptions>(...) links the section
// to the class; a class that needs it then receives IOptions<AuthOptions>
// via dependency injection. This avoids having to read strings of
// characters all over the place, as process.env.JWT_SECRET did.
// =========================================================================

namespace RdvMedecins.Config;

public class AuthOptions
{
    public const string Section = "Auth";

     // secret key used to sign/verify JWT tokens. The algorithm
     // HMAC-SHA256 requires a key of at least 256 bits, or 32 bytes.
    public string JwtSecret { get; set; } = "";

     // validity period of a token, in seconds; the cookie that carries it
     // has the same lifetime
    public int JwtExpiresInSeconds { get; set; } = 7200;

     // true in production (HTTPS): the authentication cookie is never
     // sent over an unencrypted connection
    public bool CookieSecure { get; set; }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 15: the [Auth] section of [appsettings.json], in the form of a regular class: one property per key, with the same name. This is the options template ([options pattern]) for [ASP.NET Core]. In [Program.cs], [Configure<AuthOptions>(...)] links the section to the class: the framework creates a [AuthOptions] object and populates its properties with the values from the section, converting them to the correct type (["7200"] becomes the integer 7200, [false] becomes the boolean [false]). A class that needs it receives it via dependency injection, in the form of a ***[IOptions<AuthOptions>], whose ***[Value] property is the populated object: This is what [Auth/AuthService.cs] does, with its parameter [IOptions<AuthOptions> options] and its field [auth = options.Value]. This avoids having to read character strings all over the place, as [process.env.JWT_SECRET] did in version [NestJS]: the key names are verified by the compiler, and the values are already converted;
  • line 17: the section name, written only once;
  • Lines 21–29: The three values for this section. The default values ([7200], [false] for a Boolean) are those that are used if the key is missing from the configuration.

docs.title: 11.6.6. Config/ProtectionOptions.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Config/ProtectionOptions.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The "Protection" section of appsettings.json: the protection thresholds
// against bots (see Auth/LimiteurTentativesService.cs).
// =========================================================================

namespace RdvMedecins.Config;

public class ProtectionOptions
{
    public const string Section = "Protection";

     // login: number of allowed failed attempts (incorrect CAPTCHA or password)
     // for the same login from the same address IP, before this combination is blocked...
    public int LoginMaxEchecs { get; set; } = 5;

     // ... during this period (an address IP is also blocked if it accumulates
     // 5 times as many failed attempts, across all logins)
    public int LoginBlocageMinutes { get; set; } = 15;

     // customer account creation: maximum number of accounts created per hour
     // from the same IP address. In a classroom, all workstations log out
     // often log out via the same address: increase if necessary.
    public int InscriptionMaxParHeure { get; set; } = 10;
}
  • Lines 10–25: the [Protection] section of [appsettings.json], following the same pattern. It is injected, in the form of a [IOptions<ProtectionOptions>], into [Auth/LimiteurTentativesService.cs], which reads its thresholds from it.

docs.title: 11.7.1. Program.cs
docs.text: The file [Program.cs] serves both the role of [main.ts] (startup, middleware) and that of [app.module.ts] (which service provides what) from version [NestJS]. It follows the structure of all the examples: first register the services, then build the middleware pipeline. We’ll break it down into sections.

docs.title: 11.7.1.1. The configuration
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Program.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The application’s entry point: equivalent to both main.ts
// (startup, middleware) and app.module.ts (which provides what).
//
// Two steps, always in this order:
//
//    1. builder.Services...: ENREGISTRE loads the services into the container
//       dependency injection services (the equivalent of the “providers” in the
//       NestJS). Each service has a DURÉE DE VIE:
//         - Singleton: a single instance for the entire application;
//         -    Scoped: one instance per HTTP request (the DbContext, and everything
//                       that uses it);
//         - Transient: a new instance is created each time it is requested.
//
//    2. app.Use...: the PIPELINE is constructed from the middleware components, which each
//       request passes through in the order in which they are declared.
// =========================================================================

using System.Globalization;
using System.Text.Encodings.Web;
using System.Text.Unicode;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Localization;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using RdvMedecins.Auth;
using RdvMedecins.Config;
using RdvMedecins.Data;
using RdvMedecins.Metier;
using RdvMedecins.Repositories;
using RdvMedecins.Web;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// =========================================================================
// 1. the services
// =========================================================================

// ---- typed configuration (sections of appsettings.json, see Config/)
builder.Services.Configure<AuthOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection(AuthOptions.Section));
builder.Services.Configure<ProtectionOptions>(builder.Configuration.GetSection(ProtectionOptions.Section));
var authOptions = builder.Configuration.GetSection(AuthOptions.Section).Get<AuthOptions>() ?? new AuthOptions();
  • lines 21–31: the namespaces used, in addition to the implicit [using] ones: those of the framework (localization, EF Core, encoding HTML), and those of the application, one per folder;
  • line 33: the application constructor, as in all examples. It has already read the configuration ([appsettings.json], [appsettings.Development.json], environment variables...), accessible via [builder.Configuration];
  • Lines 40–41: the options template (see [Config/AuthOptions.cs]): each section is linked to its class. [GetSection("Auth")] designates the section; [Configure<T>] registers the corresponding service [IOptions<T>], which the authentication services will receive via injection;
  • Line 42: the same section, this time read directly as an object ([Get<AuthOptions>()]), or an object with default values if the section is missing. The configuration of [JwtBearer] (below) requires the secret key right now, during service registration: at this point, the dependency injection container has not yet been built, and no [IOptions<AuthOptions>] can be injected.

docs.title: 11.7.1.2. The database and the DAO and business layers
docs.text:
// ---- Entity Framework Core: the DbContext, one per query (Scoped).
// UseMySql: the Pomelo provider for MySQL / MariaDB. The
// server version tells it which SQL dialect to generate.
var chaineConnexion = builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("RdvMedecins")
    ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("ConnectionStrings:RdvMedecins manquante dans appsettings.json");
var versionServeur = ServerVersion.Parse(builder.Configuration["MySql:ServerVersion"] ?? "8.0.0-mysql");
builder.Services.AddDbContext<RdvMedecinsDbContext>(options => options.UseMySql(chaineConnexion, versionServeur));

// ---- DAO layer and business layer: Scoped, like the DbContext on which they
// depend on (a service must never contain PLUS LONGTEMPS anything other than its dependencies)
builder.Services.AddScoped<MedecinRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<ClientRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<CreneauRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<RvRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<UserRepository>();
// "when a IMetier is requested, provide a MetierService" (NestJS:
// { provide: METIER_TOKEN, useClass: MetierService }). In C#, the interface
// itself serves as an injection token.
builder.Services.AddScoped<IMetier, MetierService>();

// ---- the cache (singleton) and its facade (scoped), see Web/ApplicationModel.cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<CacheListes>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<ApplicationModel>();
  • Lines 4–5: the connection string, as in Example 28. The operator [??] returns the value on the left if it is not [null]; otherwise, it returns the value on the right: if the key is missing, the application stops immediately, displaying a message indicating what is missing, rather than returning an obscure error on the first request;
  • line 6: the server version [MySQL], with a default value if the key is missing;
  • line 7: the application’s [DbContext] (see [Data/RdvMedecinsDbContext.cs]), one per request ([Scoped]), with the provider [MySQL] (see Example 28);
  • Lines 11–15: the DAO layer: one class per table (except for [users], whose repository is used for authentication). It is [Scoped], just like the [DbContext] it uses. A service must never outlive its dependencies: a DAO [Singleton] would retain the [DbContext] from the first request indefinitely, even though it is destroyed at the end of that request (see Chapter 6);
  • Line 19: the business layer. [AddScoped<IMetier, MetierService>()] reads: “when a service requests a [IMetier], provide it with a [MetierService].” Those who use the business layer depend on the interface, not the class: we could replace the implementation (with a test version, for example) by modifying only this line. The [NestJS] version required a token ([METIER_TOKEN]) for this, since the [TypeScript] interfaces disappear at compile time; in [C#], the interface itself serves as the token;
  • Lines 22–23: The web layer cache (the lists of doctors and clients) has application-level scope: [Singleton], a single instance shared by all requests (see Example 23). Its facade, [ApplicationModel], through which all controllers pass, uses the business layer: it is therefore [Scoped]. The cache itself, which is independent of anything else, can outlive the facade.

docs.title: 11.7.1.3. Authentication, translation, and encoding: HTML
docs.text:
// ---- authentication
builder.Services.AddScoped<AuthService>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<CaptchaService>(); // pending captchas: in memory
builder.Services.AddSingleton<LimiteurTentativesService>(); // counters: in memory
builder.Services.AddSingleton<PasseInscriptionService>(); // passes: in memory
builder.Services.AddAuthentificationJwt(authOptions); // see Auth/AuthentificationJwt.cs
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

// ---- translation
builder.Services.AddSingleton<Traducteur>();

// ---- Razor's HTML encoder. By default, it replaces any non-
// ASCII with an entity ("é" -> "é"): the page displays correctly,
// but its source code becomes unreadable. We allow it to write characters as-is
// characters from all languages; < > & " ' are always escaped.
builder.Services.AddSingleton(HtmlEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All));
  • line 2: the login service (verifying the username and password, generating the token; see Example 25). It uses the account repository: it is [Scoped];
  • Lines 3–5: pending CAPTCHAs, failure counters, and account creation passcodes (see Example 27). This data is kept in memory and must be the same for all requests: all three services are [Singleton]. The downside: they are lost every time the server restarts;
  • line 6: the configuration of [JwtBearer] (token read from the cookie, redirection to the login page...), as shown in Example 25. It is stored in an extension method of [IServiceCollection] (see [Auth/AuthentificationJwt.cs]), which is called like a framework method and thereby lightens the load on [Program.cs];
  • line 7: the authorization services, used by [[Authorize]] and by the middleware [UseAuthorization];
  • line 10: the translation service, which reads the dictionaries once and for all (see Example 22);
  • line 16: the HTML encoder from [Razor] allows characters from all languages to pass through, as in Example 15.

docs.title: 11.7.1.4. MVC and its options
docs.text:
// ---- MVC: controllers + Razor views
builder.Services.AddControllersWithViews(options =>
{
     // SessionInvalideException -> return to the login page
    options.Filters.Add<HtmlExceptionFilter>();

     // With "nullable" types enabled, MVC automatically treats a
     // string (non-nullable) property as required. We prefer to specify this ourselves,
     // explicitly, using [Required] (see Models/Formulaires.cs).
    options.SuppressImplicitRequiredAttributeForNonNullableReferenceTypes = true;

     // the error messages in LIAISON (text where a number is
     // expected: version="abc"...) are also translation keys
    var messages = options.ModelBindingMessageProvider;
    messages.SetValueMustNotBeNullAccessor(_ => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetAttemptedValueIsInvalidAccessor((_, _) => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetValueIsInvalidAccessor(_ => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetValueMustBeANumberAccessor(_ => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetUnknownValueIsInvalidAccessor(_ => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetNonPropertyAttemptedValueIsInvalidAccessor(_ => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetNonPropertyUnknownValueIsInvalidAccessor(() => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetNonPropertyValueMustBeANumberAccessor(() => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetMissingBindRequiredValueAccessor(_ => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetMissingKeyOrValueAccessor(() => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
    messages.SetMissingRequestBodyRequiredValueAccessor(() => "ERRORS.INVALID_FORM");
});
  • line 2: the [Razor] controllers and views. The function passed as a parameter sets the options for MVC;
  • line 5: a global exception filter (see Example 24), which applies to all actions. It handles only one case: a [SessionInvalideException] (the token is valid, but the account it refers to has since been deleted) leads to the login page. The other exceptions continue on their path to the [UseExceptionHandler] middleware (below);
  • line 10: a pitfall of “nullable” types. When enabled, MVC treats a (non-nullable) property [string] of a model as required, exactly as if it had the [[Required]] attribute, with an error message in English that we do not understand. This option removes this default behavior: a field is required only if it explicitly has the [[Required]] attribute, with our own message (see [Models/Formulaires.cs]);
  • Lines 14–25: binding error messages (see Example 19): text where a number is expected ([version=abc]), a missing value... Example 19 redefined only two of them, in French; the case study redefines them all, and each returns the same translation key, [ERRORS.INVALID_FORM], rather than a text: the message is translated at the time of display, in the user’s language. The character [_] refers to a parameter that is not used (the field name, the entered value): the message is the same regardless of the field. These errors should never occur with the application’s forms: they indicate a manually constructed request.

docs.title: 11.7.1.5. Loading the cache
docs.text:
var app = builder.Build();

// =========================================================================
// Cache loading (lists of doctors and clients). Scoped services
// Scoped services exist only within a "scope" (normally: a request): one is
// create one for the duration of this load. Database inaccessible -> the application
// stops here, with the exception of EF Core in the console.
// =========================================================================
using (var portee = app.Services.CreateScope())
{
    await portee.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ApplicationModel>().ChargerAsync();
}
  • Line 1: Application setup. The dependency injection container is now created: you can no longer register services, but you can retrieve them;
  • Lines 9–12: The lists of doctors and clients are loaded into the cache before the server starts listening. [ApplicationModel] is a service of [Scoped]: it can only be created within a scope, and outside of a request, there is no scope. [CreateScope()] creates one; [GetRequiredService<ApplicationModel>()] obtains the service from it (along with the business layer, the repositories, and the [DbContext] on which it depends), and [ChargerAsync()] populates the cache, which is a [Singleton] and therefore survives the scope. The [using] statement destroys the scope—and the [DbContext] along with it—when the block ends. If the database is inaccessible, the EF Core exception is not caught: the application terminates, with an error message displayed in the console. This is the first sign of an incorrect connection string or a [MySQL] server that has stopped.

docs.title: 11.7.1.6. The middleware pipeline
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 2. The middleware pipeline—the ORDRE counter
// =========================================================================

// ---- errors become HTML pages (see Web/HtmlExceptionFilter.cs):
// unhandled exception -> 500 page (the exception is logged);
// 400 / 403 / 404 response with no content -> corresponding error page
app.UseExceptionHandler("/erreur/500");
app.UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute("/erreur/{0}");

// ---- static files in the wwwroot/ directory: /css/..., /js/..., /lib/bootstrap/...
app.UseStaticFiles();

// ---- the language of each request: read from a cookie (see LangueController),
// French (default). It sets CultureInfo.CurrentCulture (date formats)
// and CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture (text language; see Web/Traducteur.cs).
var cultures = Traducteur.Langues.Select(l => new CultureInfo(l)).ToList();
var localisation = new RequestLocalizationOptions
{
    DefaultRequestCulture = new RequestCulture(Traducteur.LangueParDefaut),
    SupportedCultures = cultures,
    SupportedUICultures = cultures,
};
// only the cookie determines this (not the browser language or a setting in URL)
localisation.RequestCultureProviders = [new CookieRequestCultureProvider()];
app.UseRequestLocalization(localisation);

// ---- routing, then authentication (who is it? -> HttpContext.User, based
// based on the token), then authorization (do they have permission? -> [Authorize])
app.UseRouting();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

// ---- controllers, with their routes declared via attributes ([HttpGet("...")])
app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Each request passes through the middleware components in the order in which they are declared (see Chapter 7): this order is therefore important.

  • Line 8: The first middleware wraps all the others. If an exception has not been handled by anyone (a programming error, a database that has become inaccessible, etc.), it logs the exception and re-executes the request with the address [/erreur/500]: the user sees an application error page, not a technical message (see Chapter 7);
  • Line 9: An empty error response (400, 403, 404) is converted into a page in the same way, via the [/erreur/{code}] action of the [ErreurController] controller (see Examples 24 and 26). The re-executed request passes through the following middleware again: the error page is therefore rendered and recognizes the logged-in user;
  • line 12: the static files in the [wwwroot] folder (see Example 15): the style sheet, the page script, and [Bootstrap], stored here in [wwwroot/lib/bootstrap]. Placed early in the pipeline, this middleware responds to file requests without routing them through localization or authentication;
  • lines 17–23: the localization configuration, as in Example 22. The supported languages and the default language are those of the translation service ([Traducteur.Langues], [Traducteur.LangueParDefaut]): they are defined in only one place;
  • line 25: only the cookie set by [LangueController] determines the language (see Example 22). The syntax [[...]] is a collection expression: in this case, a list with a single element;
  • line 26: the localization middleware, which sets the language for each request;
  • lines 30–32: routing, followed by authentication, followed by authorization. Routing selects the action that will handle the request, based on the routes declared by attributes. The examples did not call it: [WebApplication] therefore adds it automatically at the beginning of the pipeline. Calling it explicitly makes the order visible: authorization must come after routing, because it is the selected action that carries the attribute [[Authorize]] to be verified; and after authentication, which determines, based on the token, who the user is (see Example 25);
  • line 35: the controllers and their routes, declared by attributes ([[HttpGet("agenda")]]...);
  • line 37: the server starts up and waits for requests on port 8081.

docs.title: 11.8. The
docs.text: The EF Core entities correspond to the database tables and the [C#] classes (see Example 28). They replicate, one by one, the [TypeORM] entities from version [NestJS]: the attributes [[Table]], [[Column]], [[Key]], [[ForeignKey]] serve as the decorators [@Entity], [@Column], [@PrimaryGeneratedColumn], and [@JoinColumn]. The database is not created by EF Core, but by the script SQL [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql]: the entities simply need to accurately describe the tables that already exist.

docs.title: 11.8.1. Entities/AbstractEntity.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Entities/AbstractEntity.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The two fields common to all entities: the identifier [id] and the
// version number [version] (optimistic lock).
//
// As with TypeORM (and @MappedSuperclass in JPA), it is sufficient for a class
// ABSTRAITE is the parent of the entity classes: EF Core does not create a table
// for it, but adds its properties to the tables of the child classes.
//
// The attributes [Key], [Column]... come from the standard namespace
// System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations: EF Core reads them to build
// its “model” (which class goes into which table, which property into
// which column). They act as decorators @PrimaryGeneratedColumn,
// @Column decorators in TypeORM.
// =========================================================================

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;

namespace RdvMedecins.Entities;

public abstract class AbstractEntity
{
     // [Key]: the primary key. By convention, an integer key is generated
     // by the database (column AUTO_INCREMENT): EF Core re-reads its value after
     // each INSERT.
    [Key]
    [Column("id")]
    public int Id { get; set; }

     // [ConcurrencyCheck]: the optimistic lock. Each UPDATE generated by EF
     // Core carries the condition "WHERE id = ... AND version = <read value>".
     // If someone has modified the line in the meantime, no line is set to
     // and EF Core raises a DbUpdateConcurrencyException.
    //
     // Difference between @VersionColumn and TypeORM: EF Core is not
     // itself an integer version number. It is our DbContext that does so,
     // just before each record (see Data/RdvMedecinsDbContext.cs).
    [Column("version")]
    [ConcurrencyCheck]
    public int Version { get; set; }
}
  • line 23: an abstract class with no attributes [[Table]]: it does not correspond to any table, but its properties are added to those of its child classes’ tables. All entities in the application inherit from it and therefore have an identifier and a version;
  • Lines 28–30: the primary key ([[Key]]), column [id]. By convention in EF Core, an integer key is generated by the database ([AUTO_INCREMENT]): EF Core re-reads its value after each [INSERT];
  • Lines 40–42: the line version for the optimistic lock (see Example 28). [[ConcurrencyCheck]] adds the condition [AND version = <valeur lue>] to each [UPDATE]. Unlike [@VersionColumn] from [TypeORM], EF Core does not increment the version itself: [DbContext] handles this (see below).

docs.title: 11.8.2. Entities/Personne.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Entities/Personne.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Parent class (without a table) of the entities [Medecin] and [Client]: a last name, a
// last name, a first name—and the associated user account (column [user]).
//
// A relationship declared in an abstract class is inherited by the
// child classes exactly as the columns: EF Core therefore adds the
// relation [User] to the table [medecins] and ET to the table [clients].
// =========================================================================

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;

namespace RdvMedecins.Entities;

public abstract class Personne : AbstractEntity
{
    [Column("titre")]
    [MaxLength(5)]
    public string Titre { get; set; } = ""; // Miss, Mrs., Mr.

    [Column("nom")]
    [MaxLength(20)]
    public string Nom { get; set; } = "";

    [Column("prenom")]
    [MaxLength(20)]
    public string Prenom { get; set; } = "";

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // The relationship to the user account, in DEUX properties—this is the
     // standard approach using EF Core:
        // - IdUser: the foreign key itself (column [user]). It can be
          // read without loading the entire User (TypeORM: @RelationId);
        // -   User: the “navigation property,” the User object itself. It
          // is populated only if requested in the query (.Include(...),
          // see Repositories/), otherwise it is null.
     // [ForeignKey] links the two. The “one-to-one” nature of the relationship
     // (column [user] UNIQUE) is specified in RdvMedecinsDbContext.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    [Column("user")]
    public int IdUser { get; set; }

     // "= null!": we promise the compiler that this property will only be read
     // when it has been loaded (Include) or assigned
    [ForeignKey(nameof(IdUser))]
    public User User { get; set; } = null!;
}
  • Line 17: the parent class—which is also abstract—of [Medecin] and [Client], itself a child of [AbstractEntity]. Doctors and clients have the same columns: they are defined only once;
  • Lines 19–29: the title (Ms., Mr., etc.), last name, and first name. [[MaxLength]] specifies the column width. These properties are of type [string] (not [string?]): they must never be set to [null], and the compiler therefore requires an initial value, in this case the empty string [""];
  • lines 42–43: the foreign key to the user account, column [user]. The account ID can be read without loading the account itself: this is what [@RelationId] did in version [NestJS];
  • lines 47–48: the navigation property: the [User] object itself. [[ForeignKey(nameof(IdUser))]] indicates which property contains the foreign key ([nameof(IdUser)] is equal to the string ["IdUser"], but the compiler verifies that the property exists). A navigation property is populated only if the query requests it ([Include]; see the DAO layer); otherwise, it is set to [null]. The notation [= null!] suppresses the compiler warning: it guarantees that the property will only be read after it has been loaded. The “one-to-one” nature of the relationship is specified in [DbContext]. A relationship declared in a parent class is inherited, just like columns: the tables [medecins] and [clients] each have their own relationship to [users].

// =========================================================================
// Entities/Medecin.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A doctor at the practice (table [medecins]).
//
// Uniqueness constraint SQL: unq_medecins_prenom_nom (two doctors
// cannot have the same first and last names) — created by the script SQL,
// identified by its name in the business layer.
// =========================================================================

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;

namespace RdvMedecins.Entities;

[Table("medecins")]
public class Medecin : Personne
{
     // inverse relationship (optional): this doctor’s appointment slots.
     // It shows the "1 doctor -> multiple time slots" relationship in both
     // directions; like any navigation, it is populated only upon request.
    public List<Creneau> Creneaux { get; set; } = [];
}
  • Line 15: The class [Medecin] corresponds to the table [medecins]. It inherits all its properties from [Personne]. The uniqueness constraint [unq_medecins_prenom_nom], mentioned in the comment, is created by the script SQL; the business layer recognizes it by its name (see Example 28);
  • line 21: the inverse relationship of that from [Creneau] to its physician: this physician’s appointment slots. EF Core automatically associates the two navigations ([Medecin.Creneaux] and [Creneau.Medecin]), which describe the same “one doctor, multiple time slots” relationship as seen from each side. Like any navigation, it is populated only on request; the application does not actually use it: it reads the appointment slots via the DAO layer. [[]] is a collection expression: in this case, an empty list.

// =========================================================================
// Entities/Creneau.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A doctor’s time slot (table [creneaux]): 8:00 a.m. – 8:20 a.m., etc.
// =========================================================================

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;

namespace RdvMedecins.Entities;

[Table("creneaux")]
public class Creneau : AbstractEntity
{
    [Column("hdebut")] public int Hdebut { get; set; } // start time of the time slot
    [Column("mdebut")] public int Mdebut { get; set; } // start minute of the time slot
    [Column("hfin")] public int Hfin { get; set; } // End hour of the time slot
    [Column("mfin")] public int Mfin { get; set; } // end minute of the time slot

     // multiple time slots for the same doctor: foreign key [id_medecin]
     // + navigation [Medecin] (same technique as Personne.IdUser / User)
    [Column("id_medecin")]
    public int IdMedecin { get; set; }

    [ForeignKey(nameof(IdMedecin))]
    public Medecin Medecin { get; set; } = null!;
}
  • lines 14–17: the hour and minute of the slot’s start and end. The attribute and property are written on the same line: this is allowed and more compact for these four similar columns;
  • Lines 21–25: the “many-to-one” relationship to the doctor: multiple time slots for one doctor. Same technique as in [Personne]: the foreign key [IdMedecin] (column [id_medecin]) and the navigation key [Medecin], linked by [[ForeignKey]]. EF Core requires no further clarification: a reference on one side, a list on the other—this is a “one-to-many” relationship.

docs.title: 11.8.6. Entities/Rv.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Entities/Rv.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// An appointment (table [rv]): a customer, in a time slot, on a given day.
//
// Uniqueness constraint SQL: unq1_rv (day, id_creneau)—a time slot is
// reserved only once per day. Created by the SQL script, identified by its
// name in the business layer.
// =========================================================================

using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.Schema;

namespace RdvMedecins.Entities;

[Table("rv")]
public class Rv : AbstractEntity
{
     // DateOnly: a date and time that exactly matches the type SQL
     // DATE in the [jour] column. (The NestJS project used a string
     // "yyyy-MM-dd": JavaScript does not have a "date without time" type.)
     // Two DateOnly values are compared directly: day < today...
    [Column("jour")]
    public DateOnly Jour { get; set; }

    [Column("id_client")]
    public int IdClient { get; set; }

    [ForeignKey(nameof(IdClient))]
    public Client Client { get; set; } = null!;

    [Column("id_creneau")]
    public int IdCreneau { get; set; }

    [ForeignKey(nameof(IdCreneau))]
    public Creneau Creneau { get; set; } = null!;
}
  • Line 15: the appointment table. Its uniqueness constraint [unq1_rv (jour, id_creneau)] ensures that a time slot is reserved only once per day;
  • Lines 22–23: the day of the appointment. The type [DateOnly] (a date without a time) corresponds exactly to the type SQL and [DATE]: no time, so no time zone issue. The [NestJS] version handled a string of type [aaaa-mm-jj], since there was no such type as [JavaScript]. Two [DateOnly] records compare directly with [<], [>=]..., in [C#] as in the [LINQ] queries;
  • Lines 25–35: the customer and the appointment time slot: two “many-to-one” relationships, each defined with a foreign key and a navigation. To create an appointment, simply populate the foreign keys [IdClient] and [IdCreneau]: this is what the business layer does.

// Entities/Role.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A user’s three roles (column users.role):
//    - ADMI N: the administrator—appointments + management of doctors and clients;
//    - DOCTOR: a doctor—books and cancels appointments;
//    - USE  R : a client (patient)—books appointments for themselves, manages their account.
//

// ('ADMIN' | 'DOCTOR' | 'USER'): the compiler rejects any other value.

// the SQL script (see HasConversion<string>() in RdvMedecinsDbContext).

namespace RdvMedecins.Entities;

public enum Role
{
    ADMIN,
    DOCTOR,
    USER,
}
  • lines 17–21: the three roles, in the form of an enumeration ([enum]): A variable of type [Role] can only take the values [Role.ADMIN], [Role.DOCTOR], or [Role.USER], and the compiler rejects any other value. This is equivalent to the string union type ['ADMIN' | 'DOCTOR' | 'USER'] from version [NestJS]. By default, EF Core would store a base enumeration as a number (0, 1, 2); the [role] column contains text: the conversion is requested in [DbContext].

docs.title: 11.9. The DbContext
docs.text: The [DbContext] in the application is based on the one from Example 28, with five tables instead of one, and a few clarifications about the model that the attributes cannot express.

docs.title: 11.9.1. Data/RdvMedecinsDbContext.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Data/RdvMedecinsDbContext.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// DbContext is the core component of Entity Framework Core. It acts as the
// the following role:
//    - the DataSource of TypeORM: the database connection;
//    - the Repository<T>s of TypeORM: one DbSet<T> per table, which
//      is queried in LINQ (db.Medecins.Where(...)...);
//    - a “unit of work”: it SUIT the entities it has
//      loaded (change tracking). When a property is modified, nothing
//      is sent to the database; it is SaveChangesAsync() that sends, in a single batch, the
//      INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE required.
//
// Lifetime: one DbContext per HTTP request (“scoped” record,
// see Program.cs). All repositories within the same request therefore share
// the MÊME DbContext—and consequently the same connection and the same
// transaction when the business layer opens one.
//
// The class-to-table mapping is described primarily by the attributes
// of the entities ([Table], [Column], [ForeignKey]...) ; OnModelCreating supplements
// what the attributes cannot convey.
// =========================================================================

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;

namespace RdvMedecins.Data;

public class RdvMedecinsDbContext(DbContextOptions<RdvMedecinsDbContext> options) : DbContext(options)
{
     // one "table" per entity. Set<T>() returns the DbSet that EF Core created
     // for type T.
    public DbSet<Medecin> Medecins => Set<Medecin>();
    public DbSet<Client> Clients => Set<Client>();
    public DbSet<Creneau> Creneaux => Set<Creneau>();
    public DbSet<Rv> Rvs => Set<Rv>();
    public DbSet<User> Users => Set<User>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder)
    {
         // A doctor (a customer) has a UN account, and an account belongs to at most
         // UNE person (column [user] UNIQUE in the script SQL):
         // "one-to-one," whose foreign key is carried by medecins.user
         // (clients.user). Without this clarification, EF Core would assume “multiple
         // doctors for the same account”—which would also work, but
         // would not accurately describe the model.
        modelBuilder.Entity<Medecin>().HasOne(m => m.User).WithOne().HasForeignKey<Medecin>(m => m.IdUser);
        modelBuilder.Entity<Client>().HasOne(c => c.User).WithOne().HasForeignKey<Client>(c => c.IdUser);

         // The role is a C# enumeration, stored in the database as text
         // ('ADMIN', 'DOCTOR', 'USER') rather than as numbers (0, 1, 2)
        modelBuilder.Entity<User>().Property(u => u.Role).HasConversion<string>();
    }

    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // The optimistic lock (see AbstractEntity.Version): just before each
     // record, the version of every entity is incremented MODIFIÉE.
     // EF Core compares the ANCIENNE value (the one read from the database) in the clause
     // WHERE of the UPDATE, and writes the new one:
          // UPDATE doctors SET name = ..., version = 4 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 3
    //
     // ChangeTracker: the "track changes" for DbContext. It knows, for
     // for each loaded entity, whether it was added (Added), modified
     // (Modified), deleted (Deleted), or left unchanged (Unchanged).
    //
     // All variants of SaveChanges(Async) lead to this method.
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public override Task<int> SaveChangesAsync(bool acceptAllChangesOnSuccess, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
    {
        foreach (var entree in ChangeTracker.Entries<AbstractEntity>())
        {
            if (entree.State == EntityState.Modified)
            {
                entree.Entity.Version++;
            }
        }
        return base.SaveChangesAsync(acceptAllChangesOnSuccess, cancellationToken);
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 29: As in Example 28, the [DbContext] receives its options ([MySQL] provider, connection string) from [AddDbContext], within [Program.cs]. It is registered with the [Scoped] lifetime: one [DbContext] per request, shared by all repositories for that request, meaning a single connection and, if applicable, a single transaction. It thus fulfills the roles of both the [DataSource] and the [Repository<T>] for [TypeORM];
  • Lines 33–37: one [DbSet] per table. There are none for either [AbstractEntity] or [Personne]: these abstract classes have no tables. EF Core does not include them in the model as entities; it simply adds their properties to those of the child classes;
  • Line 39: [OnModelCreating] is called once, when EF Core constructs its model (the description of tables and relationships). It supplements the entity attributes with a fluid API: a chain of method calls;
  • Lines 47–48: The relationship between a doctor (a customer) and their account is “one-to-one”: [HasOne(m => m.User)] (a doctor has one account), [WithOne()] (an account has at most one doctor; the empty parentheses indicate that [User] has no reverse lookup), [HasForeignKey<Medecin>(m => m.IdUser)] (the foreign key is in table [medecins]). Without these rows, EF Core would assume a “many-to-one” relationship (multiple doctors for a single account), which would also work but would inaccurately describe the model: in the database, the [user] column is unique;
  • line 52: [HasConversion<string>()] stores the role in the database as text (['ADMIN']...), and converts it back to [Role] upon reading;
  • lines 68–77: the version number of each modified entity is incremented just before saving, as in Example 28. [ChangeTracker.Entries<AbstractEntity>()] iterates through all tracked entities whose class derives from [AbstractEntity]: thanks to the common parent class, this single loop applies to all five tables. The variant of [SaveChangesAsync] is redefined with two parameters, because it is this variant that ultimately calls [SaveChangesAsync()] without parameters. EF Core compares the old version in the [WHERE] clause of [UPDATE] and writes the new one: if the line has changed in the meantime, no lines are modified, and EF Core raises a [DbUpdateConcurrencyException].

docs.title: 11.10. The domain: the calendar
docs.text: The [Domain] file contains two classes that do not correspond to any tables: they describe a doctor’s schedule for a single day, calculated by the business layer ([MetierService.GetAgendaMedecinJourAsync]) and displayed by the schedule controller.

docs.title: 11.10.1. Domain/CreneauMedecinJour.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Domain/CreneauMedecinJour.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A "business" object (without a table) that associates a time slot with the
// any appointment that may be scheduled during that time slot on a given day.
//
// A C# “record” is a class whose properties are set once
// by the constructor (immutable object): exactly what’s needed
// for a computed object that no one modifies afterward.
// =========================================================================

using RdvMedecins.Entities;

namespace RdvMedecins.Domain;

// Rv?: null if the time slot is available on that day
public record CreneauMedecinJour(Creneau Creneau, Rv? Rv);
  • Line 17: a time slot, and the appointment scheduled for that time slot on that day, [null] if the time slot is available (hence the type [Rv?]). A [record] written this way, with its parameters in parentheses (positional record), declares in a single line a class, its constructor, and its properties [Creneau] and [Rv], which cannot be modified after construction: This is equivalent to the [constructor(public creneau: Creneau, ...)] syntax in the [NestJS] version. We have already encountered the records for data passed to the business layer (see Example 28).

namespace RdvMedecins.Domain;

The schedule (line 14): a doctor, a day, and the list of their available or booked time slots, in chronological order.

docs.title: 11.11. The DAO layer
docs.text:
One class per table, as in Example 28: short methods, without business logic, that simply query or modify the database. Here, they are called “repositories,” as in the version [NestJS]. Two differences from that version:

  • queries are written in [LINQ], which EF Core translates into SQL: you navigate from one entity to another using navigation properties, and EF Core writes the joins itself;
  • The methods have no [manager] parameter for transactions: all repositories in a query share the same [DbContext], and a transaction opened on this [DbContext] by the business layer automatically encompasses all their queries.

All methods are asynchronous and return a [Task]: the caller waits for it with [await]. Many are written in the form [=> expression]: they directly return the [Task] for the request, without [async] or [await], since they have nothing else to do afterward.

docs.title: 11.11.1. Repositories/PersonneRepository.cs
docs.text:
In version [NestJS], the repositories for doctors and clients were identical, except for a single line. In [C#], a generic class writes them once.

// =========================================================================
// Repositories/PersonneRepository.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The DAO layer shared by doctors and clients.
//
// The two DAO from the NestJS project (MedecinRepository, ClientRepository)
// were identical except for one line. In C#, a class named GÉNÉRIQUE writes them
// only once: PersonneRepository<T>, where T is either Doctor or Client.
// "where T : Person" ensures that T has LastName, FirstName, User...
//
// Transactions: methods no longer require the parameter EntityManager
// optional parameter from TypeORM. All repositories in a request share the
// MÊME DbContext (see Data/RdvMedecinsDbContext.cs): when the business layer
// opens a transaction on this DbContext, all of its queries automatically become part of
// as part of the transaction.
// =========================================================================

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using RdvMedecins.Data;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;

namespace RdvMedecins.Repositories;

public abstract class PersonneRepository<T>(RdvMedecinsDbContext db) where T : Personne
{
    protected readonly RdvMedecinsDbContext db = db;

     // the "table" of people of type T (db.Medecins or db.Clients)
    protected DbSet<T> Table => db.Set<T>();

     // a list sorted by last name then first name, including the user ID.
     // Include(p => p.User): retrieves the account (AUSSI) via a join
     // (SELECT ... FROM doctors INNER JOIN users ...). Without it, p.User
     // would be null.
     // AsNoTracking(): these lists are stored in memory by the cache
     // (Web/ApplicationModel.cs), well beyond the request HTTP: it is unnecessary
     // (and costly) for DbContext to follow them.
    public Task<List<T>> FindAllAsync() =>
        Table.AsNoTracking().Include(p => p.User).OrderBy(p => p.Nom).ThenBy(p => p.Prenom).ToListAsync();

    public Task<T?> FindByIdAsync(int id) =>
        Table.Include(p => p.User).FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == id);

     // the person whose user account is [idUser], or null
    public Task<T?> FindByUserIdAsync(int idUser) =>
        Table.Include(p => p.User).FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.IdUser == idUser);

     // the person with that first and last name, if there is one. The comparison
     // is performed by MySQL, using the database’s collation
     // (utf8mb4_unicode_ci: ignoring uppercase letters and accents) —
     // follows exactly the same rule as the uniqueness constraint SQL.
    public Task<T?> FindByPrenomNomAsync(string prenom, string nom) =>
        Table.FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Prenom == prenom && p.Nom == nom);

     // creation (Id = 0: not yet in the database) or modification (entity already
     // followed by DbContext: SaveChanges detects the changes on its own)
    public async Task<T> SaveAsync(T personne)
    {
        if (personne.Id == 0)
        {
            Table.Add(personne);
        }
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
        return personne;
    }

     // ExecuteDeleteAsync (EF Core 7+): a DELETE sent directly to the database,
     // without loading the entities fi rst: DELETE FROM doctors WHERE id = ?
    public Task DeleteByIdAsync(int id) => Table.Where(p => p.Id == id).ExecuteDeleteAsync();
}

// the two concrete DAO: everything is inherited
public class MedecinRepository(RdvMedecinsDbContext db) : PersonneRepository<Medecin>(db);

public class ClientRepository(RdvMedecinsDbContext db) : PersonneRepository<Client>(db)
{
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     // reads a client by placing a VERROU on its line until the end of the
     // current transaction (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE). A second transaction
     // that requests the same lock ATTEND as the first must be completed.
     // Used for scheduling appointments (see MetierService.AjouterRvAsync):
     // Two simultaneous appointments for the same patient are thus processed
     // one is APRÈS and the other is LINQ, and the second reservation sees the appointment created by the first.
    //
     // LINQ cannot express “FOR UPDATE”: we write the query SQL
     // ourselves. FromSqlInterpolated transforms {id} into PARAMÈTRE SQL (not
     // string concatenation, so no SQL injection is possible).
    // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    public async Task<Client?> VerrouillerAsync(int id)
    {
        var clients = await Table.FromSqlInterpolated($"SELECT * FROM clients WHERE id = {id} FOR UPDATE").ToListAsync();
        return clients.FirstOrDefault();
    }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Line 24: [PersonneRepository<T>] is a generic class; [T] is a type parameter, replaced by an actual type ([Medecin] or [Client]) when the class is used, such as [T] in [List<T>]. The constraint [where T : Personne] only accepts [Personne] or its child classes for [T]: the compiler then knows that a [T] contains [Id], [Nom], [Prenom], [IdUser], [User]... and accepts [p.Nom] in queries. The class is abstract: only its two child classes, listed below, are used;
  • line 26: the [db] parameter of the main constructor is visible only within this class. It is copied to a field named [protected] so that the child classes ([ClientRepository]) can access it;
  • line 29: the table of persons of type [T]. [db.Set<T>()] maps [DbSet] to this type: [db.Medecins] for [T = Medecin], [db.Clients] for [T = Client];
  • lines 38–39: all individuals, sorted by last name then first name ([OrderBy], then [ThenBy] to break ties for identical last names). [Include(p => p.User)] also loads each person’s account via a join ([INNER JOIN users]): without it, [p.User] would be equivalent to [null]. The count is used to display the login in the lists. [AsNoTracking()] (see Example 28): these lists are kept in memory by [ApplicationModel] long after the query has ended; there is no need for [DbContext] to process them. Expressions such as [p => p.Nom] are not executed in [C#]: EF Core parses them to translate them into SQL ([ORDER BY nom, prenom]);
  • lines 41–42: a person and their account, or [null]. Here, there is no [AsNoTracking()]: the business layer modifies the retrieved person (and their account), then calls [SaveAsync]; the [DbContext], which tracks both objects, knows what has changed;
  • lines 45–46: the person whose account is [idUser]. This is how a logged-in patient, whose token contains the account ID, retrieves their customer record. The filter targets the foreign key itself ([WHERE clients.user = ...]); the join with [users] serves only to load the account ([Include]);
  • lines 52–53: a possible homonym. The operator [==] is converted to [=] SQL: the comparison is performed using [MySQL], according to the database’s collation, without regard to uppercase letters or accents, exactly as in the uniqueness constraint (see Example 28). A comparison using [C#] would take uppercase letters into account;
  • Lines 57–64: Creation or modification, as in Example 28: A new person ([Id] set to 0) is added to [DbSet]; a person already in the system requires no action. Note: [SaveChangesAsync] logs all pending changes for [DbContext], not just those from [personne]: the account modified at the same time is included in the same call;
  • line 69: deletion via [ExecuteDeleteAsync] (see example 28): a [DELETE] sent directly to the database, without prior reading. It does not go through change tracking, nor therefore through the optimistic lock;
  • line 73: the doctors’ repository: [PersonneRepository<Medecin>], with nothing else. It forwards the received [DbContext] to the constructor of its parent class; the final semicolon replaces an empty class body;
  • line 75: the client repository, with an additional method;
  • lines 89–92: reading a client with a lock: [SELECT ... FOR UPDATE] places a lock on the line until the end of the current transaction; another transaction requesting the same lock waits until the first one is complete. The appointment scheduling method ([MetierService.AjouterRvAsync]) uses this to process two simultaneous reservations for the same patient one after the other: the second reservation sees the appointment created by the first and thus complies with the “only one upcoming appointment” rule. [LINQ] cannot express [FOR UPDATE]: you must write the query SQL yourself using [FromSqlInterpolated]. The string [$"..."] is an interpolated string; [FromSqlInterpolated] does not copy it as-is: each value enclosed in curly braces ([{id}]) becomes a parameter SQL. Therefore, there is no string concatenation, and no SQL injection is possible. The query is executed as-is ([ToListAsync]), and the first client in the resulting list ([FirstOrDefault], in memory): an operator [LINQ] added after [FromSqlInterpolated] would cause EF Core to wrap our SQL in a subquery.

docs.title: 11.11.2. Repositories/CreneauRepository.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Repositories/CreneauRepository.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Layer DAO of the entity [Creneau].
// =========================================================================

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using RdvMedecins.Data;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;

namespace RdvMedecins.Repositories;

public class CreneauRepository(RdvMedecinsDbContext db)
{
    public Task<Creneau?> FindByIdAsync(int id) =>
        db.Creneaux.Include(c => c.Medecin).FirstOrDefaultAsync(c => c.Id == id);

     // A doctor’s appointment slots, in chronological order
    public Task<List<Creneau>> GetAllCreneauxAsync(int idMedecin) =>
        db.Creneaux
            .Where(c => c.IdMedecin == idMedecin)
            .OrderBy(c => c.Hdebut)
            .ThenBy(c => c.Mdebut)
            .ToListAsync();

     // Deletes all of a doctor’s time slots (removal of a doctor):
        // DELETE FROM slots WHERE id_medecin = ?
    public Task DeleteByMedecinAsync(int idMedecin) =>
        db.Creneaux.Where(c => c.IdMedecin == idMedecin).ExecuteDeleteAsync();
}
  • lines 15–16: an appointment slot, with its doctor ([Include]);
  • lines 19–24: a doctor’s time slots, in chronological order: [Where] filters, [OrderBy] and [ThenBy] sort (by hour, then by start minute). The query is built method by method, as with QueryBuilder from [TypeORM], and is executed only when [ToListAsync] is called: [SELECT ... FROM creneaux WHERE id_medecin = @p ORDER BY hdebut, mdebut]. The value [idMedecin] is also passed as a parameter to SQL;
  • Lines 28–29: Deleting a doctor’s appointment slots using a single [DELETE]. The business layer calls it before deleting the doctor; otherwise, the foreign key [creneaux.id_medecin] would prevent the deletion.

docs.title: 11.11.3. Repositories/RvRepository.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Repositories/RvRepository.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Layer DAO of the entity [Rv] (an appointment).
//
// Queries are written in LINQ: EF Core translates them into SQL. Navigation
// from one entity to another using the navigation properties (rv.Creneau.IdMedecin),
// and EF Core writes the necessary joins itself.
// =========================================================================

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using RdvMedecins.Data;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;

namespace RdvMedecins.Repositories;

public class RvRepository(RdvMedecinsDbContext db)
{
    public Task<Rv?> FindByIdAsync(int id) =>
        db.Rvs.Include(rv => rv.Client).Include(rv => rv.Creneau).FirstOrDefaultAsync(rv => rv.Id == id);

    public async Task<Rv> SaveAsync(Rv rv)
    {
        if (rv.Id == 0)
        {
            db.Rvs.Add(rv);
        }
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
        return rv;
    }

    public Task DeleteByIdAsync(int id) => db.Rvs.Where(rv => rv.Id == id).ExecuteDeleteAsync();

     // a doctor’s appointments on a given day, including the patient and time slot.
     // rv.Creneau.IdMedecin: The table [rv] does not directly reference the
     // doctor; EF Core uses a join with [creneaux].
    public Task<List<Rv>> GetRvMedecinJourAsync(int idMedecin, DateOnly jour) =>
        db.Rvs
            .Include(rv => rv.Client)
            .Include(rv => rv.Creneau)
            .Where(rv => rv.Creneau.IdMedecin == idMedecin && rv.Jour == jour)
            .ToListAsync();

     // a customer’s appointments starting on or after the date [depuis] (inclusive), in
     // in chronological order, with the time slot ET and the doctor for that time slot
     // (Include, then ThenInclude: appointment -> time slot -> doctor)
    public Task<List<Rv>> FindAVenirByClientAsync(int idClient, DateOnly depuis) =>
        db.Rvs
            .Include(rv => rv.Creneau).ThenInclude(c => c.Medecin)
            .Where(rv => rv.IdClient == idClient && rv.Jour >= depuis)
            .OrderBy(rv => rv.Jour)
            .ThenBy(rv => rv.Creneau.Hdebut)
            .ThenBy(rv => rv.Creneau.Mdebut)
            .ToListAsync();

     // number of appointments for a client starting from day [depuis] (inclusive)
    public Task<int> CountAVenirByClientAsync(int idClient, DateOnly depuis) =>
        db.Rvs.CountAsync(rv => rv.IdClient == idClient && rv.Jour >= depuis);

     // deletes TOUS a client’s appointments (past and future):
        // DELETE FROM rv WHERE id_client = ?
    public Task DeleteByClientAsync(int idClient) =>
        db.Rvs.Where(rv => rv.IdClient == idClient).ExecuteDeleteAsync();

     // number of appointments (past or future) for a doctor:
        // SELECT COUNT(*) FROM appointment INNER JOIN time slots c ON ... WHERE c.id_medecin = ?
    public Task<int> CountByMedecinAsync(int idMedecin) =>
        db.Rvs.CountAsync(rv => rv.Creneau.IdMedecin == idMedecin);
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 19–20: an appointment with a client and its time slot: two [Include] records, so two joins;
  • lines 22–29: same pattern as for people. In practice, it is used only for creation: the business layer generates a [Rv] in which only the foreign keys are populated; after [SaveChangesAsync], [rv.Id] contains the identifier assigned by the database;
  • line 32: canceling an appointment;
  • Lines 37–42: A doctor’s appointments for a given day, each with its own patient and time slot (the equivalent of [leftJoinAndSelect] in the [NestJS] version). The [rv] table does not directly reference doctors: the [rv.Creneau.IdMedecin == idMedecin] filter goes through the [Creneau] navigation, and EF Core adds the join with [creneaux]. It is important to distinguish between the two uses of a navigation: in [Where], it is used for filtering; only [Include] loads the object into the result;
  • lines 47–54: a client’s appointments starting from the day [depuis], along with their time slot and the doctor for that slot: [Include(rv => rv.Creneau)] loads the time slot, then [ThenInclude(c => c.Medecin)] loads the doctor for that time slot (two cascading joins). The sort is based first on the day, then on the time of the time slot. This is what is displayed in “My Account”;
  • lines 57–58: the number of these appointments ([SELECT COUNT(*)]), for the rule “only one upcoming appointment.” [CountAsync] directly satisfies the condition, as does [FirstOrDefaultAsync];
  • lines 62–63: the deletion of all of a client’s appointments, past and future: the business layer calls this before deleting the client, which the foreign key [rv.id_client] would otherwise protect;
  • lines 67–68: the number of appointments for a doctor, to prevent the deletion of a doctor who has any. Once again, the [rv.Creneau] navigation generates a join ([INNER JOIN creneaux]) without loading anything: this is the [innerJoin] from the [NestJS] version.

docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Repositories/UserRepository.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Layer DAO of entity [User]. Create (or delete) a physician or a
// client also creates (or deletes) their account—see Metier/MetierService.cs.
// =========================================================================

using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using RdvMedecins.Data;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;

namespace RdvMedecins.Repositories;

public class UserRepository(RdvMedecinsDbContext db)
{
     // null if no user has this login
    public Task<User?> FindByLoginAsync(string login) => db.Users.FirstOrDefaultAsync(u => u.Login == login);

    public async Task<User> SaveAsync(User user)
    {
        if (user.Id == 0)
        {
            db.Users.Add(user);
        }
        await db.SaveChangesAsync();
        return user;
    }

    public Task DeleteByIdAsync(int id) => db.Users.Where(u => u.Id == id).ExecuteDeleteAsync();
}
  • line 17: the account associated with this login, or [null]. It is used for logging in ([AuthService]) and to verify that a login is available before assigning it;
  • Lines 19–26: Creating or modifying an account. To create a doctor or a client, you must first create their account: the person needs the account ID for their foreign key;
  • line 29: Deleting an account. The order is the reverse of the creation process: the business layer first deletes the person, who references the account, and then deletes the account.

docs.title: 11.12. The Business Layer
docs.text: The business layer contains the application’s business rules: no appointments in the past, only one upcoming appointment per patient, unique usernames and individuals, and the deletion of a doctor or a client. It relies on the DAO layer (folder [Repositories]) for reading and writing, and knows nothing about HTML or the interface language. More specifically, this is the [PersonnesMetier] layer from Example 28.

docs.title: 11.12.1. Business/Dates.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Business/Dates.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Today’s date. It is used for RÈGLES, DE, and GESTION (no appointment
// in the past; only one appointment per patient at VENIR): it therefore resides
// in the business layer. The web layer reuses it.
// =========================================================================

namespace RdvMedecins.Metier;

public static class Dates
{
     // today’s date, in the server’s time zone
    public static DateOnly Aujourdhui() => DateOnly.FromDateTime(DateTime.Now);
}
  • line 11: a [static] class is not instantiated; it simply groups methods, which are called by the class name ([Dates.Aujourdhui()]);
  • line 14: today’s date, in the server’s time zone. [DateTime.Now] returns both the date and time; [DateOnly.FromDateTime] returns only the date (the type [DateOnly] was covered in Example 12; this is the format of the [rv.jour] column). Two [DateOnly] values can be compared directly with [<] or [>=]; the [NestJS] version, which processed [aaaa-mm-jj] strings, had to generate this format itself. The current date is used for business rules, so it resides in the business layer; the web layer reuses it (for example, in [AgendaController], to determine whether a day is still bookable).

docs.title: 11.12.2. Business/MetierException.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Business/MetierException.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The exception thrown by the business layer when a RÈGLE DE GESTION is
// violated (username already taken, doctor still has appointments, time slot
// already booked...). It does not carry text, but a CLÉ of
// translation (e.g., "ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN"): it is the web layer that
// will translate into French or English when the page is displayed
// (see i18n/fr.json, i18n/en.json).
//
// A MetierException is not an error: it is a normal response
// ("this login is already taken"), displayed to the user. Any other
// exception is a true error, which results in a 500 error page.
// =========================================================================

namespace RdvMedecins.Metier;

public class MetierException(string cle, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>? parametres = null) : Exception(cle)
{
     // message translation key
    public string Cle { get; } = cle;

     // any message parameters ({minutes}...)
    public IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> Parametres { get; } = parametres ?? new Dictionary<string, string>();
}
  • Line 18: The exception thrown when a business rule rejects a transaction (see Example 28). The class uses a primary constructor (the parameters [cle] and [parametres] are listed after the class name); [: Exception(cle)] passes the key to the constructor of the parent class [Exception], which sets it as the property [Message] (useful in error logs). Difference from Example 28: The exception does not carry text in French, but rather a translation key ([ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN]). The business layer thus ignores the interface language: it is the web layer that will translate the key, using the dictionaries [i18n/fr.json] and [i18n/en.json] (see Chapter 5);
  • line 21: the translation key, read-only ([get] without [set]);
  • line 24: any message parameters, which will replace markers such as [{minutes}] in the translated text. [IReadOnlyDictionary] is a read-only dictionary. The [??] operator returns an empty dictionary when no parameters are provided: the web layer never needs to check for [null]. The exceptions thrown by [MetierService] actually only use keys without parameters.

A [MetierException] is not an error: it is a normal response (“this login is already taken”), which controllers intercept to display to the user, either on the page or in a pop-up message. Any other exception is a true error, which results in a 500 error page.

docs.title: 11.12.3. Metier/IMetier.cs
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// Business Layer/IMetier.cs
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The business layer contract: readings, calendar, appointments, management
// of doctors and clients.
//
// Convention .NET: an asynchronous method returns a Task<T> (the equivalent
// of a Promise<T>) and its name ends with "Async".
// =========================================================================

using RdvMedecins.Domain;
using RdvMedecins.Entities;

namespace RdvMedecins.Metier;

// the data entered in the “doctor” or “client” form
public record DonneesPersonne
{
    public required string Titre { get; init; } // Mr., Mrs., Ms.
    public required string Nom { get; init; }
    public required string Prenom { get; init; }

     // creation: optional; defaults to the name in lowercase
     // modification: optional; the login remains unchanged if it is missing
    public string? Login { get; init; }

     // creation: optional; defaults to the username
     // modification: optional; the password remains unchanged if omitted
    public string? Password { get; init; }

     // modification: the version of the record at the time the form was
     // displayed (optimistic lock, see AbstractEntity.Version)
    public int? Version { get; init; }
}

public interface IMetier
{
     // ------------------------------------------------ readings
    Task<List<Client>> GetAllClientsAsync();
    Task<List<Medecin>> GetAllMedecinsAsync();
    Task<List<Creneau>> GetAllCreneauxAsync(int idMedecin);
    Task<List<Rv>> GetRvMedecinJourAsync(int idMedecin, DateOnly jour);
    Task<Client?> GetClientByIdAsync(int id);
    Task<Medecin?> GetMedecinByIdAsync(int id);
    Task<Rv?> GetRvByIdAsync(int id);
    Task<Creneau?> GetCreneauByIdAsync(int id);
    Task<AgendaMedecinJour?> GetAgendaMedecinJourAsync(int idMedecin, DateOnly jour);

     /// <summary>the client (patient) whose user account is [idUser], or null</summary>
    Task<Client?> GetClientByUserIdAsync(int idUser);

     /// <summary>a client’s appointments, for today or in the future, with time slot and doctor</summary>
    Task<List<Rv>> GetRvAVenirClientAsync(int idClient);

     // ------------------------------------------------ appointments (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER)
     /// <summary>
     /// triggers a MetierException if:
      /// - the day has passed ("ERRORS.PAST_DATE");
      /// - the patient already has an upcoming appointment ("ERRORS.PATIENT_HAS_UPCOMING_APPOINTMENT");
      /// - the time slot is already booked for that day ("ERRORS.SLOT_ALREADY_BOOKED").
     /// </summary>
    Task<Rv> AjouterRvAsync(DateOnly jour, Creneau creneau, Client client);

    Task SupprimerRvAsync(Rv rv);

     // ------------------------------------------------ doctors (ADMIN)
     /// <summary>creates the doctor ET's user account (role DOCTOR)</summary>
    Task<Medecin> AjouterMedecinAsync(DonneesPersonne donnees);

     /// <summary>modifies the doctor ET’s user account</summary>
    Task<Medecin> ModifierMedecinAsync(int id, DonneesPersonne donnees);

     /// <summary>deletes the doctor, his time slots, and his account ET—rejected if he has appointments</summary>
    Task SupprimerMedecinAsync(int id);

     // ------------------------------------------------ clients
     // (ADMIN; AjouterClientAsync is also used to register a patient,
     // ModifierClientAsync and SupprimerClientAsync for the patient to manage their own account)
     /// <summary>creates the client ET and their user account (role USER)</summary>
    Task<Client> AjouterClientAsync(DonneesPersonne donnees);

    Task<Client> ModifierClientAsync(int id, DonneesPersonne donnees);

     /// <summary>
     /// deletes the client, their account ET, and all their appointments (past and future).
     /// Used by ADMIN (the "Clients" page) and by the patient themselves ("Manage My Account").
     /// </summary>
    Task SupprimerClientAsync(int id);
}
  • Lines 17–33: Data for a doctor or client to be created or modified, as transmitted by the web layer (see Example 28). [required] requires the title, last name, and first name; [init] prevents these from being modified later (see Example 18). Username and password are optional ([string?]): upon creation, they default to the name in lowercase; upon modification, they change only if they have been entered. [Version] is the version of the record read when the edit form is displayed: it is used for optimistic locking (see below);
  • line 36: the business layer’s contract: what other layers can request from it, without specifying how it is done (interfaces were discussed in Example 06). By convention, [.NET], an asynchronous method returns a [Task<T>] (the equivalent of a [Promise<T>] of [JavaScript]) and its name ends with [Async];
  • lines 39–53: the readings. A type followed by [?] ([Task<Client?>]) indicates that the method can return [null]: no one has this identifier. The comments for [/// <summary>] are documentation comments: [Visual Studio Code] displays them when you hover over the method;
  • lines 57–64: appointments. The comment for [AjouterRvAsync] lists the possible error codes: this is part of the contract that testers must be familiar with;
  • lines 68–74: doctor management (reserved for ADMIN). Each doctor is created, modified, and deleted along with their user account;
  • lines 80–88: client management, following the same logic. [AjouterClientAsync] is also used to register a patient, while [ModifierClientAsync] and [SupprimerClientAsync] are for patients who manage their own accounts.

The implementation is recorded in [Program.cs] via line [builder.Services.AddScoped<IMetier, MetierService>()]: “When a manufacturer requests a [IMetier], provide them with a [MetierService],” one per request ([Scoped]), such as [DbContext] and the DAO entries it uses (see Example 28 and Chapter 6). With [NestJS], a [TypeScript] interface disappeared at compile time: a token ([METIER_TOKEN]) and [@Inject(METIER_TOKEN)] were required. In [C#], the interfaces exist at runtime: the interface itself serves as the token. The only service that receives a [IMetier] is [ApplicationModel] (folder [Web]), which also implements [IMetier]: the controllers therefore see the same contract, enriched with a cache of lists of doctors and clients.
